clue.text: Present exercise not mastered

indicators.note: as an imperative, exercise tells you to put these letters through their paces, working them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A drill being handed out now is one that nobody has yet got the hang of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exercise' reads as a noun but is an instruction: work the letters of NOT MASTERED into a new order. 'Present' is the verb, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to present a new product to an audience is to show it off publicly.

clue.text: 1-0 up, caught for 5: cause of serious complaint

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom towards the top
caught for 5 means the first thing stands in place of the second

parts.note: a score of one-nil is called one-love in tennis, written I LOVE with the Roman numeral for one
V is the Roman numeral for five
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A team leading by a goal then has its fifth batsman caught, which causes a formal protest.
explanation.walkthrough: One-love is I LOVE; 'caught for 5' swaps its V for C, giving ILOCE, and 'up' turns that to run from the bottom. The complaint is an illness, not a protest.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this gut bacterium is a well-known source of severe food poisoning, and a complaint is an ailment.

clue.text: Swimmer in row following his splashing

parts.note: to row a boat is to oar it
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

indicators.note: splashing suggests the letters being thrown about into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a rowing boat follows a man who is thrashing about in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splashing' rearranges HIS into ISH. 'Swimmer' is the crossword habit of describing a fish by what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a very long ribbon-like sea fish, and any fish can be called a swimmer.

clue.text: Maxim supporting view that has its ups and downs

definitions.text: that has its ups and downs

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the other and holds it up

parts.note: to view something is to see it
a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: A guiding principle backs up an opinion whose fortunes rise and fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporting' puts the maxim below the word for view in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: the playground plank tips so each end rises and falls in turn.

clue.text: Sort of umbrella blown in

definitions.meaning: a tightly furled brolly, the kind once carried by City gents in London
informal for arrived casually, turned up unannounced

explanation.definitionFit: One phrase describes a furled brolly and, informally, having arrived somewhere.

clue.text: Drink heavily with jerry turning up in a sleeveless garment

parts.note: to tank is slang for to drink a great deal

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a jerry is old British slang for a chamber pot

explanation.surface: Someone boozes hard alongside a German who arrives wearing a vest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' makes POT read upwards as TOP. A jerry is old British slang for a chamber pot, not a German soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a knitted or jersey vest with no arms.

clue.text: Do shorter novel about the yard, for example? I did!

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the other pieces
novel as an adjective means new, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written
say is used to mean for instance

explanation.surface: A suggestion to write a briefer book about Scotland Yard, from an author who did just that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges DO SHORTER into DOROTHERS, and 'about' wraps it round Y and SAY. 'I did!' points back at the whole surface: she wrote detective fiction featuring Scotland Yard.
explanation.definitionFit: The crime writer who created Lord Peter Wimsey produced detective stories involving police from Scotland Yard.

clue.text: Second-class it spares — they don't make a dramatic difference

definitions.text: they don't make a dramatic difference

parts.note: B is the grade below A, so second-class
taken as written
spares are replacement components for a machine

explanation.surface: Travelling in the cheaper carriage saves on things that hardly matter anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dramatic' is literal: this is about the theatre, not about size of effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: these are small roles in a play that barely affect the drama.

clue.text: Buy pastry for teacher and gain advantage initially

parts.note: to buy something is to get it
a head is a head teacher in a British school, and a tart is a pastry, so whimsically a head's tart, written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Purchase a cake for the schoolmaster and you will be in favour from the off.
explanation.walkthrough: A head is a British head teacher; the pastry belonging to one is A HEAD'S TART, respaced to make the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to begin a race or contest already in front of rivals.

clue.text: Overdrawn for a time on trip creating a stink

indicators.note: one thing for another means the first replaces the second
on says the swap is carried out upon the word that follows, the trip

parts.note: a tour is a trip round several places
T is the abbreviation for time
OD is the bank statement abbreviation for overdrawn

explanation.surface: Being in the red for a while on holiday causes a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps the T of TOUR for OD, and 'on' says which word the swap is made in. A stink in the surface is a fuss; the answer is a literal smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: a stink is a strong, usually unpleasant, smell.

clue.text: Rose's home situated in jolly elegant surroundings

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is simply a kind of rose

indicators.note: situated in places one piece within the surroundings formed by the other
jolly suggests merry or tipsy, so the letters are in disorder

parts.note: taken as written
in means at home

explanation.surface: A woman called Rose has a house set in very stylish grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' (the anagram signal) gives EGLANTE, which 'situated in ... surroundings' wraps round the home. In the surface jolly is the British intensifier meaning very.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is another name for the sweet briar, a wild flowering shrub with pink blooms.

clue.text: Set up one drink during discourse

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so the pieces sit within the other word

parts.note: to discourse is to speak at length, to orate
I is the Roman numeral for one
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: Somebody pours a single glass while a long speech goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' is the insertion signal. 'discourse' reads as a noun, a talk, but is the verb meaning to speak at length.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to found or start something, to bring it into being.

clue.text: Strong personality showing what online solvers would do at 15

parts.note: people solving on a screen enter letters with a keyboard, so they type
the entry at 15 in this grid begins with the letter A, which is what you would key in there

explanation.surface: A forceful character demonstrates the method of internet crossword fans at number fifteen.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue points at the grid itself: square 15 holds an A, so a solver on a keyboard would key that letter there.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychology label: the driven, competitive, impatient character in the well-known two-way classification.

clue.text: Like moorland well out of line

indicators.note: out of means one piece is taken away from the other

parts.note: well as an adjective means in good health

explanation.surface: Countryside resembling a moor lies a long way off the bus route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' takes L from HEALTHY. 'well' reads as an adverb meaning far, but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive adjective: covered in heather and low scrub, as open upland is.

clue.text: Reebok perhaps for worker on run

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a worker is one caste of ant
to elope is to run away, usually to marry

explanation.surface: Sports shoes from a famous brand, ideal for an employee out jogging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' stacks the worker above the word for run. Reebok is an alternative spelling of rhebok, a South African animal; the trainer brand is named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the reebok or rhebok is a species of this swift horned grazing animal.

clue.text: Damn pockets put off old thief (not me!)

indicators.note: as a verb, pockets means takes inside itself

parts.note: to damn someone is to curse them

indicators.note: off means gone bad or awry, so the letters are disturbed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wretched trouser pouches deterred a pickpocket of long ago, and the speaker denies being one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges PUT into UTP and 'pockets' has CURSE take it in. 'pockets' looks like a noun but is the verb; '(not me!)' is the setter's joking disclaimer.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic term: a pickpocket of earlier centuries who sliced money bags from belts.

clue.text: A shop assistant, first person going from city down under

indicators.note: going from means one piece leaves the other

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a food shop
I is the first person singular pronoun
an aide is an assistant

explanation.surface: A sales clerk, the earliest to leave an Australian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going from' removes I from DELI, leaving DEL. 'first person' is grammatical: the pronoun I.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is the capital of South Australia.

clue.text: Head of agribusiness seeds it? Not exactly

definitions.text: Head of agribusiness seeds it? Not exactly

indicators.note: not exactly says the letters are not in precisely this order
the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Does the boss of a farming company sow this land? Quite the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not exactly' rearranges A (from 'Head of' agribusiness) with SEEDS IT. The whole clue also defines: under the EU scheme farmers were paid to leave such land unsown.
explanation.definitionFit: Farming term: land deliberately taken out of production and left unsown, under a former European subsidy scheme.

clue.text: Working at mains sustained energy

indicators.note: working suggests the letters being manipulated into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Running off the electricity supply gave continuous power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' rearranges AT MAINS. 'sustained' looks like a verb but is an adjective in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: staying power, the ability to keep going over a long effort.

clue.text: Reviled Republican president ensnares us Democrat

indicators.note: ensnares means traps, so one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: Abe Lincoln was the first Republican president of the USA
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hated right-wing leader lures a liberal politician from our side into a trap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ensnares' has ABE take in US. 'Reviled' reads as an adjective on the president but is a past tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a past tense: insulted or spoke to with harsh, offensive language.

clue.text: Whisper put about in spa town, west and east

indicators.note: put, with the later 'in', says one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: Bath is an English city famous for its Roman hot springs
re means concerning or about

explanation.surface: A rumour is spread around both ends of a resort with healing waters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put ... in' is the insertion signal, and 'west and east' says where things land: the word for about goes near the start of the English spa city, and east closes the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to utter very quietly, as in 'don't say a word of it'.

clue.text: Boring goods in raised American garden

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
in a down clue, raised means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Americans call a house's garden the yard
G abbreviates good, so the plural goods gives two of them

explanation.surface: Tedious merchandise is displayed in an elevated plot in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' makes the American garden read DRAY in this down entry, and 'in' is the insertion signal for the goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: tediously slow and dull.

clue.text: Conference location next to place taken over

indicators.note: taken over means turned over, so the whole run is read from its far end

parts.note: at can mean beside, as in 'at my side'
to place something down is to lay it

explanation.surface: A meeting venue beside a site that has been bought out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken over' turns AT plus LAY end to end. 'place' is a verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical example: the Crimean resort where Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met in 1945.

clue.text: Criminal is central suspect

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious or unreliable, so the letters are not to be trusted in this order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawbreaker is the main person the police have in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' rearranges IS CENTRAL. 'Criminal' is a noun here, though it is so often the anagram signal itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a thief, one who commits the offence of stealing property.

clue.text: Pub with computer stuff that produces stress for some

parts.note: an inn is a pub
IT is information technology

explanation.surface: A bar full of gadgets, which makes certain customers anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: The stress is emphasis, not anxiety: this British slang tag, short for 'isn't it', is added to a sentence to underline it.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a British slang tag, short for 'isn't it', tacked on by certain speakers for emphasis.

clue.text: Putting right agent on broadcast

indicators.note: on means added to, so the pieces are joined one after the other

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative or agent
an airing is a transmission of a programme

explanation.surface: Correcting a spy live on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' is a noun here, a showing of a programme, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a participle: mending or fixing what is broken.

clue.text: Singer's ready for an audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is taken by ear and not by spelling

parts.note: ready, or the ready, is British slang for cash, and a tenner is a ten-pound note

explanation.surface: A vocalist is prepared to perform for the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is British slang for cash: a ten-pound note is a TENNER, which 'for an audience' says is heard, not seen.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a man with a high voice, such as Pavarotti.

clue.text: Straps left by seats for fixing?

indicators.note: for fixing means in need of repair, so the letters are to be put into proper order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Restraints lying beside car chairs, waiting to be attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for fixing' rearranges LEFT BY SEATS. The whole clue paints the answer too: straps beside seats, there to be fastened.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: restraints worn across the body in cars and aircraft.
